title: What is the Kingdom of God?
aliases: kingdom of god in the bible
summary: The kingdom of God is the rule God brings about. In the cited passages it is announced by Jesus, prayed for by his followers, described in terms of righteousness and peace, and finally portrayed as God's lasting reign. The texts include both present response and future completion.
historical_context: The references trace the theme through different kinds of biblical writing: Psalm 2 portrays the LORD's anointed king, Daniel 2 contrasts God's lasting kingdom with earthly kingdoms, Mark 1 records Jesus announcing that the kingdom has drawn near, and later New Testament passages describe its ethical and future dimensions. This is a map of the cited texts, not a comparison with every ancient idea of kingship.
canonical_context: Daniel 2:44–45 pictures God's kingdom as one that will not be destroyed. Mark 1:14–15 brings the theme into Jesus' announcement: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom has drawn near, and his hearers are called to repent and believe. Matthew 6:9–13 makes its coming a subject of prayer; Romans 14:17 describes it through righteousness, peace, and joy; and 1 Corinthians 15:24–28 and Revelation 11:15 look toward its final establishment. These passages show present response and future hope without making them identical.
literary_context: The theme appears in several forms. Psalm 2 is a royal psalm; Daniel 2 presents a vision interpreted as a sequence of kingdoms; Mark 1 gives a summary of Jesus' proclamation; Matthew 6 places the kingdom in a prayer; Romans 14 uses it to address community life; and 1 Corinthians 15 and Revelation 11 describe its final horizon. The genre and immediate argument explain why the kingdom can refer to both God's active rule and its future completion.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect God's rule with the life and hope of his people. Jesus calls hearers to respond with repentance and faith (Mark 1:14–15); the Lord's Prayer asks for the kingdom to come (Matthew 6:9–13); and Paul describes kingdom life through righteousness, peace, and joy (Romans 14:17). First Corinthians 15:24–28 then speaks of the kingdom's completion when opposing powers are brought to an end. The texts hold ethical life and future hope together.
canonical_role: What is the Kingdom of God? serves as a question-oriented anchor, connecting common reader language to related passages, themes, and CKL entries.

related_objects.notes: the kingdom comes through the Messiah

interpretive_notes.note: The cited texts describe more than private feeling: Mark 1 calls for public allegiance expressed in repentance and faith, while Romans 14:17 connects kingdom life with how a community lives together. They also do not reduce the kingdom to a human political program.

Mark 1:14–15 presents the kingdom as having drawn near, while 1 Corinthians 15:24–28 and Revelation 11:15 speak of its final reign. Keep the different time horizons visible rather than forcing one passage to answer every question about timing.
